title: Finite-type reduced toric realizations and their smooth tori
statement: Let $M$ be a fine torsion-free monoscheme admitting a finite affine cover, and form $X=\mathbf Q[M]$ with its component tori and coactions as in [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. Then $X$ is reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme] and of finite type over $\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. It has finitely many connected components, each integral. On each component the generic group $L$ is a finitely generated free abelian group of finite rank $r$, and $T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q[L]$ is isomorphic as a group scheme to $\mathbf G_m^r=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, with multiplication and unit given by multiplying coordinates and the coordinates $1$. In particular $T$ is a smooth finite-type $\mathbf Q$-group [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] acting on that component by the indicated coaction. For every reduced finite-type $\mathbf Q$-scheme $Y$, $T\times_{\mathbf Q}Y$ is reduced and of finite type, and its projection to $Y$ is smooth and surjective. The assertions about reducedness, finite type and finitely many components also hold for finite disjoint unions of such realizations.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 3.1.4 and 3.1.10(ii), Proposition 3.2.2 and 3.2.4--3.2.5, printed pp.98--100,103; smooth torus input in 2.3.16--2.3.17 and application in 3.2.19. No Stacks tag states the complete monoscheme realization assertion.

proof.text: First examine the finite monoid charts in [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup] and [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. A prime ideal of a monoid generated by $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ is determined by which generators it contains: a sum belongs to the prime ideal exactly when some summand does. Thus its spectrum is finite. The empty prime is contained in every prime, so its point $\eta$ belongs to every nonempty basic open; its stalk inverts all generators and is $P^{\rm gp}$. In a finite affine cover the underlying space of $M$ is therefore finite. For any $x\in M$, all its generalizations lie in any affine chart containing $x$; that chart has the unique generic point just described. It is the unique generic point generalizing $x$ in $M$: any generalization lies in the same chart and specializes from its empty prime. Denote it by $\eta(x)$. On each affine chart $\eta(x)$ is constant. Consequently the sets $M_\eta=\{x:\eta(x)=\eta\}$ are open and closed, cover $M$, and are finite in number. Each is the closure of its point $\eta$, hence irreducible and connected. They are exactly the connected components. Each affine chart lies in just one $M_\eta$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 3.1.4(i)--(ii) and Remark 3.1.10(ii), printed pp.98--100; explicit prime-ideal argument.

proof.text: On a nonempty component choose an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}_{\rm mon}P$. Its generic stalk is $L=\mathcal M_\eta=P^{\rm gp}$ by Step 1, and the same stalk identifies every other chart's group completion with $L$. Finitely many generators of $P$ generate $P^{\rm gp}$ as a group. Torsion-freeness of the stalk group completion is an assumption on $M$ in [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. Apply [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free] to obtain a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ of $L$. This verifies both hypotheses of that node without assuming that $P$ is saturated or sharp.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.1.9 and 3.2.4, printed pp.99,103; finite free generic lattice used also in the proof of Lemma 3.2.12(ii), p.104.

proof.text: For each chart $P$, apply [lem-trf-affine-monoid-algebra-normalization] with $k=\mathbf Q$. Its hypotheses hold because $P$ is fine and $P^{\rm gp}=L$ is torsion free. In particular $\mathbf Q[P]$ is an integral domain. Hence every localization at a prime is reduced: if $(a/s)^n=0$ in a localization of a domain then $a=0$. The chart realizations cover $X$ by [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization], so all local rings of $X$ are reduced, precisely [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Independently, if $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ generate $P$, their monomials generate $\mathbf Q[P]$ as a $\mathbf Q$-algebra, since $e^{\sum a_i p_i}=\prod(e^{p_i})^{a_i}$. The finite monoid-chart cover gives a finite affine cover of $X$ by these finitely generated algebras. This is finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism].

source.place: Expose VIII, Proposition 3.2.2, 3.2.4 and Lemma 3.2.12(ii), printed pp.103--104; domain and algebra-generator arguments.

proof.text: The disjoint clopen decomposition of Step 1 is respected by realization: its gluing uses no overlap between different $M_\eta$, by [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. Write $X_\eta=\mathbf Q[M_\eta]$. On a chart with generators $p_i$, put $a=\sum_i p_i$ (use $a=0$ if there are none). Inverting $a$ inverts each $p_i$, because $-p_i=-a+\sum_{j\ne i}p_j$; thus $P[a^{-1}]=L$. The ring identification $\mathbf Q[P]_{e^a}=\mathbf Q[L]$ sends $e^p/(e^a)^n$ to $e^{p-na}$, with the inverse given by the same fraction rule. These are the localization maps used in gluing, so every chart of $X_\eta$ contains the same open $T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q[L]$. It is dense in each chart: the zero prime of the domain $\mathbf Q[P]$ belongs to $D(e^a)$ and to every nonempty open. The zero prime of $\mathbf Q[L]$ likewise makes $T$ irreducible. Every nonempty open of $X_\eta$ therefore meets $T$, and any two such opens meet, since their intersections with $T$ do. Thus $X_\eta$ is irreducible and nonempty. Step 3 makes it reduced, hence integral by [def-pc-integral-scheme]. The finitely many $X_\eta$ are consequently exactly the connected components of $X$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Proposition 3.2.2 and 3.2.4, printed p.103; dense torus and component argument expanded from Remark 3.1.10(ii).

proof.text: The basis from Step 2 gives inverse ring maps $\mathbf Q[L]\rightleftarrows\mathbf Q[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$ by $e^{\sum n_i b_i}\mapsto\prod t_i^{n_i}$ and $t_i\mapsto e^{b_i}$. They preserve products and the unit by the unique integer-coordinate expressions, so [def-weil-affine-spectrum] gives the required scheme isomorphism. The torus coaction, counit and inverse send $e^l$ respectively to $e^l\otimes e^l$, $1$ and $e^{-l}$; in these coordinates they are coordinate multiplication, the tuple $(1,\ldots,1)$ and coordinate inversion. The group identities hold on every $e^l$. Each component is torsion free, since its stalks are stalks of the assumed torsion-free $M$; Step 2 identifies its generic group with the finite free $L$. Thus the torsion-free connected-component hypothesis of [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization] holds. The chart action is its specified coaction; its action and unit identities follow on $e^p$ from $e^p\otimes e^p\otimes e^p$ and $e^p$. Localization respects these formulas: when $e^a$ is inverted, its coaction is inverted to $e^{-a}\otimes e^{-a}$. Hence the actions agree on overlaps and give the stated action on $X_\eta$. The displayed scheme isomorphism respects the group operations.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.2.4--3.2.5, printed p.103; group law and coaction on the monomial basis.

proof.text:
Fix any $\mathbf Q$-scheme $Y$ for the moment. Over $V=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq Y$, the projection $T\times_{\mathbf Q}Y\to Y$ has algebra $R[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, as can be checked by its functor of points using [def-pc-fibre-product] and [def-weil-affine-spectrum]: a map to this affine scheme is a map to $V$ and $r$ units. This algebra has the finite presentation
$$R[t_1,\ldots,t_r,u_1,\ldots,u_r]/(t_i u_i-1\mid1\le i\le r).$$
These affine preimages cover the product. Thus the projection is locally of finite presentation in exactly the sense of [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. If $Y$ is finite type over $\mathbf Q$, take its finite affine cover by finitely generated $\mathbf Q$-algebras as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Adjoining these $2r$ generators gives a finite such cover of $T\times Y$, so the product is finite type. For $Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q$ this also proves finite type of $T$.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.2.4 and Lemma 3.2.12(i), printed pp.103--104; Laurent presentation over an arbitrary base written explicitly.

proof.text: For formal smoothness of the same projection take a first order affine thickening $\operatorname{Spec}(B/J)\subset\operatorname{Spec}B$ over $Y$, with $J^2=0$ as in [def-sbc-first-order-thickening]. By Step 5, a map from $\operatorname{Spec}(B/J)$ to $T$ is $r$ units $\bar v_i\in B/J$. Choose lifts $v_i,w_i\in B$ of $\bar v_i$ and their inverses. Then $v_iw_i=1+j_i$, $j_i\in J$, and $v_i$ is a unit with inverse $w_i(1-j_i)$ because $j_i^2=0$. The lifted units give a map $\operatorname{Spec}B\to T$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Pair it with the prescribed map to $Y$ using [def-pc-fibre-product]; it lifts the given map to $T\times Y$ and lies over $Y$. This is the formal lifting condition in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Together with Step 6 it proves the projection smooth, also when $Y$ is not affine. Taking $Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q$ proves $T$ smooth over $\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12(i), printed p.104, the polynomial/Laurent smoothness calculation; explicit first-order unit lifts.

proof.text: Evaluation $t_i=1$ is the identity section $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q\to T$ from Step 5. Pairing it with the identity of any $Y$ by [def-pc-fibre-product] gives a section $Y\to T\times Y$ of the projection. Thus the projection is surjective on underlying points: a point $y$ is the image of its image under the section. This includes $r=0$ (the projection is an identity) and $Y=\varnothing$.

source.place: Expose VIII, 2.3.16--2.3.17 and 3.2.19, printed pp.95,106; the torus projection is smooth and surjective, with its section displayed.

proof.text: It remains to check reducedness of the product for reduced $Y$. Put $A=\mathbf Q[L]$. For every extension field $K/\mathbf Q$, the basis map $A\otimes_{\mathbf Q}K\to K[L]$, $e^l\otimes c\mapsto ce^l$, is an isomorphism; its inverse sends $ce^l$ to $e^l\otimes c$. The monoid $L$ is fine and its group completion is torsion free, so [lem-trf-affine-monoid-algebra-normalization] with $P=L$ and $k=K$ says $K[L]$ is a domain, hence reduced. For any affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R$ in the reduced scheme $Y$, $R$ is reduced by [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Apply [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-base-change] to $A$ and $R$: it gives reducedness of $R\otimes_{\mathbf Q}A$. The affine product chart of Step 6 is precisely $\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_{\mathbf Q}A)$, via $r\otimes e^l\mapsto re^l$. A localization of a reduced ring is reduced: if $(b/s)^n=0$, some denominator $u$ has $ub^n=0$, whence $(ub)^n=0$ and $ub=0$. Therefore every local ring of the product is reduced. These charts cover it, proving reducedness in [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. No irreducibility assumption on $Y$ was used.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.2.4 and 3.2.19, printed pp.103,106; reducedness of the torus product justified by the existing general reduced tensor-product lemma.

proof.text: Finally let $X=\coprod_{j=1}^s X_j$ be a finite disjoint union of the realizations already treated. Its local ring at a point of $X_j$ is that in $X_j$, so it is reduced by [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. The union of the finitely many finite affine covers supplied by Step 3 is a finite affine cover by finitely generated $\mathbf Q$-algebras, giving finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A connected subset lies in one summand, because the summands are open and closed; hence its connected components are the components of the summands. There are finitely many by Step 4. For an empty monoscheme or an empty disjoint union all these assertions are vacuous, with zero connected components; all the rank-zero formulas above remain valid.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.1.3, Remark 3.1.10(ii), and finite-disjoint-union convention in 3.1.26, printed pp.98--100,102.
